notes.b: Every species does a particular job in its ecosystem (a community of living things together with their non-living surroundings). That job, and the way of life that goes with it, is called its niche.
points: The niche of a species is its role, or functional position, in its ecosystem. It includes what it feeds on and what feeds on it, where in the habitat it lives and feeds, and when it is active.

The niche also includes the range of abiotic conditions (non-living factors such as temperature, moisture, light and pH) the species can tolerate, its interactions with other species, and its effects on its environment.
Habitat and niche differ. The habitat is where an organism lives, its address; the niche is how it lives there, its profession. Many species share one habitat, but each has its own niche.

Example: in an oak woodland, caterpillars feed on the leaves, woodlice and earthworms feed on dead leaves on the floor, blue tits eat caterpillars in the canopy, and fungi decompose fallen wood. One habitat, five different niches.

A species' niche is the result of its adaptations. Its structural, behavioural and physiological features (its body structure, its behaviour and the way its body works) suit it to a particular way of life, and they also limit it to that way of life.
notes.tip: Habitat and niche are not the same thing, and examiners ask you to distinguish them: say where it lives (habitat) against how it lives there (niche). A niche is more than what an organism eats, so include where, when, the conditions tolerated and its interactions. Adaptations arise by natural selection, not because the organism needs them.

notes.b: Because a niche is a set of resources and conditions, two species that want the same ones are in direct competition. Whether they can live side by side depends on how much their niches overlap.
points: Competitive exclusion: two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche in the same place for long. They compete for the same resources, and the better-adapted species wins while the other declines or is excluded locally.

Example: the grey squirrel and the red squirrel have similar niches in Irish woodland, as tree-living seed and nut eaters. In broadleaf woodland the grey squirrel is larger and can feed efficiently on acorns that red squirrels digest poorly, so it outcompetes the red squirrel.
The red squirrel survives better in conifer woodland, where the grey squirrel's advantage with acorns counts for less.

Niche differentiation: similar species can live together if their niches differ, for example by feeding on different foods, at different heights or at different times of day. This reduces competition between them.

Example: in the same grassland, the kestrel hunts small mammals by day and the barn owl hunts them at night. Both occur in Ireland, and sharing the same prey does not put them in competition because they hunt at different times.
notes.tip: If asked what happens when two species have the same niche, say they compete for the same resources and the better-adapted one wins while the other declines or is excluded locally. Give the grey and red squirrel as your example.

notes.b: Niches vary in width. A narrow niche can make a species very efficient but fragile, while a broad niche makes a species flexible.
points: A specialist has a narrow niche, depending on one food or one habitat. This makes it efficient at using that resource but vulnerable to change, because it has nothing to fall back on.
Example: the caterpillars of the marsh fritillary butterfly feed mainly on one plant, devil's-bit scabious, so the butterfly depends on the wet grasslands and bogs where that plant grows.
A generalist has a broad niche. The red fox eats rabbits, mice, birds, insects, earthworms, fruit and scraps, and lives in countryside and towns, so it copes well with change.
An invasive species (one that spreads and thrives after arriving in a new area) is often one that finds a niche unfilled, or fills an existing niche better than the native species, in its new home.
The grey squirrel is an example of an invasive species. There is more on this in Biodiversity loss and conservation.
notes.tip: When asked why a specialist is at risk, link the narrow niche to its dependence on one food or habitat, and use the marsh fritillary. Contrast it with the red fox as a generalist.

notes.h: Describing a niche in an exam
notes.b: Questions often ask you to describe the niche of a named organism. A niche is built from several parts, so cover each of them rather than only the food.
points: State the organism's ecosystem and habitat, then its trophic level (its feeding position in the food chain) and what it eats.
Say what eats it, and when and where it is active, so that its place in the food web and its daily pattern are both clear.
State the conditions it tolerates, then give two or three adaptations, each matched to the part of its niche it suits.
notes.tip: Examiners ask you to describe the niche of a named organism and explain how two adaptations suit it to that niche. Name the adaptation, then say what it does for the organism. Legacy questions also asked for examples of structural and behavioural adaptations with their benefits.

notes.h: Sundew: niche and adaptations (raised and blanket bogs)
notes.b: Bog peat is waterlogged, acidic and very short of nitrogen, which plants need to build proteins. The sundew solves this by photosynthesising like other plants but also catching insects to get the nitrogen it lacks.
points: Niche: a producer that photosynthesises in waterlogged, acidic bog where the peat is very poor in nitrogen, and that supplements its nitrogen by catching and digesting insects.
Adaptation: leaves bearing red hairs (tentacles), each tipped with a drop of sticky fluid that glistens, attracts small insects and traps them.
Adaptation: the tentacles bend over the trapped insect, holding it against the leaf.
Adaptation: glands secrete enzymes that digest the insect, and the leaf absorbs the products, including nitrogen compounds. This makes up for the nitrogen-poor peat.
Adaptation: a small rosette of leaves close to the ground, in an open, sunny habitat, which suits its photosynthesis and the insects that land on it.
Diagram: a sundew leaf with sticky tentacles curved over a trapped insect. Labels: leaf, tentacle, sticky drop, trapped insect.
notes.tip: The sundew traps insects to get nitrogen, not to get energy: it is a producer and still photosynthesises, so the peat is poor in nitrogen and the insects make up the shortfall.

notes.b: On a rocky shore, the tide brings waves, predators and drying out in turn. The limpet is a grazer built to hold on, to avoid drying out and to scrape up its food.
points: Niche: a primary consumer (grazer) that scrapes the thin film of algae off rocks between the tides. It is eaten by birds such as oystercatchers and by crabs.
Adaptation: a low, conical shell that waves flow over without dislodging it.
Adaptation: a strong muscular foot that clamps the limpet to the rock against waves and predators.
Adaptation (behavioural): at low tide it clamps down onto its own home scar, a groove ground into the rock to match its shell. This seals in water and prevents drying out.
Adaptation: a rough, tongue-like radula that rasps algae from the rock.
Adaptation (behavioural): it feeds when covered by the tide and returns to its home scar, so it is always back in its sealed position when the tide goes out.
notes.tip: Name each adaptation and say what it does: shape against waves, foot against waves and predators, home scar against drying out, radula for feeding. Remember to mark which are structural and which are behavioural.

notes.h: Barn owl: niche and adaptations (farmland and grassland)
notes.b: The barn owl hunts in the dark, so it relies on silence, hearing and night vision more than on sight in daylight. Its adaptations suit each part of that hunting niche.
points: Niche: a nocturnal predator (secondary or tertiary consumer) of small mammals such as mice, rats and shrews, nesting in old buildings and hollow trees.
Adaptation: soft feathers with fringed, comb-like edges on the flight feathers make its flight almost silent, so prey does not hear it coming.
Adaptation: a heart-shaped facial disc of feathers funnels sound to the ears.
Adaptation: ears at slightly different heights on each side of the head, so it can locate prey by sound alone in darkness.
Adaptation: large, forward-facing eyes give binocular vision (both eyes view the same scene, which helps judge distance) in dim light.
Adaptation: sharp, curved talons and a hooked beak grip and tear prey.
notes.tip: Pick two adaptations and link each to catching prey in the dark, for example fringed feathers for silent flight, or asymmetric ears to locate prey by sound.

notes.h: Bumblebee or honeybee: niche and adaptations (grassland, meadows, hedgerows and gardens)
notes.b: Bees feed on flowers and in doing so carry pollen between them, so their niche is tied to flowering plants. Their body structure and behaviour suit collecting food and moving pollen.
points: Niche: a primary consumer that feeds on nectar (energy) and pollen (protein), and a pollinator of flowering plants, transferring pollen from flower to flower. There is more on this in Flower structure and pollination.
Adaptation: a long, tube-like tongue (proboscis) to reach nectar inside flowers.
Adaptation: a hairy body to which pollen sticks, which is how pollen is carried from flower to flower.
Adaptation: pollen baskets, stiff hairs on the hind legs, carry pollen back to the nest.
Adaptation: eyes that see the ultraviolet patterns on petals, which guide the bee to nectar.
Adaptation (behavioural): honeybees communicate the location of flowers to others by a dance.
notes.tip: The dance is a behavioural adaptation; the proboscis, hairy body and pollen baskets are structural. Give the benefit of each one when asked.

notes.h: Earthworm: niche and adaptations (soil of grassland and woodland)
notes.b: The earthworm lives in the soil, eating dead plant material, so it recycles nutrients. Its body is built for burrowing and for breathing through its skin in damp ground.
points: Niche: a detritivore (an animal that eats dead leaves and other dead organic matter) feeding on dead leaves and soil organic matter, recycling nutrients.
Its burrows aerate and drain the soil and it mixes the soil layers. It is also food for blackbirds, thrushes, badgers and foxes.
Adaptation: a long, thin, segmented body without legs for burrowing.
Adaptation: tiny bristles (chaetae) on each segment grip the burrow wall.
Adaptation: mucus lubricates movement and binds the burrow walls.
Adaptation: a thin, moist skin exchanges gases, so the earthworm lives in damp soil and comes to the surface mainly at night or in wet weather.
Adaptation (behavioural): it pulls leaves into its burrow, so it feeds below ground, away from predators.
notes.tip: Link the thin, moist skin to gas exchange and to the earthworm's need for damp soil. Structural adaptations here are the body shape, chaetae, mucus and skin; pulling leaves into the burrow is behavioural.

notes.h: Marram grass: niche and adaptations (sand dunes)
notes.b: Sand dunes are dry, salty and shifting, so few plants can live there. Marram grass is a pioneer, the first plant to colonise bare ground, and its adaptations suit it to these harsh conditions.
points: Niche: a pioneer producer that colonises loose, dry, salty sand and binds it into dunes, allowing other plants to settle later. There is more on plant water loss in Transport in Plants.

Adaptation: leaves roll into a tube in dry conditions, with stomata (the pores in the leaf) on the inner surface in grooves lined with hairs. This traps moist air and reduces water loss by transpiration.
Adaptation: long roots reach water deep in the sand.
Adaptation: underground stems (rhizomes) spread and bind the sand.
Adaptation: it grows upward when it is buried by blowing sand, so it is not smothered.
notes.tip: For marram grass, link rolled leaves, hairy grooves and sunken stomata to reduced water loss, and long roots to reaching deep water.

keyTerms.definition: The role of a species in its ecosystem, including what it feeds on, where and when it is active, the conditions it tolerates and its interactions with other species.
The principle that two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche in the same place for long, so the better-adapted species wins and the other declines or is excluded locally.
The way similar species live together because their niches differ, e.g. in their food, height or time of activity.
A species with a narrow niche, such as one food or one habitat, which makes it efficient but vulnerable to change.
A species with a broad niche, which allows it to feed on many foods and live in many habitats, so it copes well with change.
A structural, behavioural or physiological feature that suits an organism to its way of life and niche.
A species that colonises bare or loose ground first, such as marram grass on sand dunes.
A non-native species introduced by people that spreads and harms native species and ecosystems.
The place where an organism lives, which provides the food, shelter and conditions it needs.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a habitat and a niche, using one organism as an example.
questions.model: A habitat is the place where an organism lives, the organism's address, and it provides food, shelter and conditions. A niche is the organism's role in the ecosystem, the way it lives there, including what it feeds on, what eats it, when it is active and the conditions it tolerates. For example, the limpet's habitat is the rocky shore, but its niche is that of a primary consumer, a grazer that scrapes algae off rocks between the tides and is eaten by oystercatchers and crabs.

questions.prompt: Outline the concept of the niche. Describe the niche of one named animal and one named plant and explain how three adaptations suit each to its niche.
questions.model: The niche of a species is its role in its ecosystem, including what it feeds on and what feeds on it, where and when it is active, the conditions it tolerates and its interactions with other species. It differs from the habitat, which is only where the organism lives. Animal, the limpet on the rocky shore: its niche is a primary consumer that grazes algae between the tides, and it is eaten by oystercatchers and crabs. Its adaptations are a low, conical shell that waves flow over without dislodging it, a strong muscular foot that clamps it to the rock, and a home scar that it returns to at low tide, which seals in water and prevents drying out. Plant, the sundew in raised and blanket bogs: its niche is a producer on waterlogged, acidic, nitrogen-poor peat that supplements its nitrogen by digesting insects. Its adaptations are red glandular tentacles, each tipped with sticky fluid that traps insects, tentacles that bend over the trapped insect, and enzymes that digest the insect so the leaf can absorb the nitrogen compounds.

questions.prompt: Red squirrels and grey squirrels occupy similar niches. Explain what happens when they live in the same woodland, and why the red squirrel survives better in some woodlands than others.
questions.model: Red squirrels and grey squirrels are tree-living seed and nut eaters with similar niches. Two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche in the same place for long, so they compete for the same resources, and the better-adapted species wins. In broadleaf woodland the grey squirrel is larger and can feed efficiently on acorns, which red squirrels digest poorly, so it outcompetes the red squirrel. The red squirrel survives better in conifer woodland, where the grey squirrel's advantage on acorns does not apply. The grey squirrel is also an invasive species, which often finds a niche unfilled or fills an existing niche better than the native species in its new home.
